This winter I went digging into the Hebrew Roots movement and its claims.

The movement promotes Christians keeping the Sabbath on Saturday instead of Sunday, using “Yeshua” instead of “Jesus,” following dietary laws, observing Passover and Sukkot, and claiming that Western Christianity was corrupted by Rome and Constantine, arguing that they are restoring the authentic faith by returning to Jewish roots.

They’re right about the corruption part.

I spent all of last year documenting how Rome systematically edited, suppressed, and distorted Scripture. How the 66-book Protestant canon is incomplete. How the Ethiopian Orthodox Church preserved the 81-book canon, including 1 Enoch, which Jude directly quotes as Scripture. How institutional Christianity has been shaped more by Roman political interests than apostolic teaching.

So when Messianic Judaism says “Western Christianity was corrupted,” I don’t dismiss it. That’s demonstrably true.

But just because Rome corrupted the faith doesn’t mean Hebrew Roots has the correct restoration.

Diagnosing the disease correctly doesn’t guarantee the cure is legitimate. And the more I researched this winter, reading their materials, comparing claims to Scripture, tracing the historical parallels, the more questions surfaced. Questions that make me wonder if this movement escaped one corruption only to adopt another.

I’ll be examining Messianic Judaism and the Hebrew Roots movement in depth. But before I do, you need context. You need to know what you’re actually looking at, the history, the claims, and the questions that keep surfacing when you dig beneath the surface.

What Is Messianic Judaism?

At its simplest, Messianic Judaism is Jews who believe Jesus (Yeshua) is the Messiah while maintaining Jewish identity and Torah observance.

The modern movement emerged in the 1960s and 70s as ethnically Jewish believers in Jesus began asking: “Do we have to stop being Jewish to follow our Messiah?” The answer they arrived at was no. They could be both, Jewish in practice, Christian in belief.

Messianic Judaism blends Christian soteriology (salvation through Jesus) with Jewish practice (Sabbath, dietary laws, festivals, synagogue worship). It’s distinct from Hebrew Roots, though the two overlap significantly. Hebrew Roots is primarily Gentiles adopting Jewish practices, claiming they’re “grafted into Israel” and therefore obligated to live like Jews.

Today, estimates suggest 300,000-500,000 people worldwide identify with Messianic Judaism or Hebrew Roots. The movement is growing, especially online, where YouTube channels, Substacks, and social media amplify the message.

Which makes it worth examining carefully.

Two Timelines: Ancient and Modern

To understand what’s happening today, you need to know this isn’t new. There are actually two histories here.

Ancient Jewish Christianity (1st-4th Century)

The earliest church was thoroughly Jewish. The apostles were Jews. The first believers were Jews. They worshiped in the temple, kept Torah, observed Sabbath. Christianity began as a Jewish sect, not a separate religion.

But tension emerged almost immediately.

When Gentiles started believing in Jesus, a question arose: Do they need to become Jewish (circumcision, Torah observance) to be part of the covenant? The Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 addressed this head-on. The apostles’ decision: No. Don’t burden Gentiles with Torah beyond four specific things, abstaining from food sacrificed to idols, blood, strangled animals, and sexual immorality (Acts 15:28-29).

Paul fought this battle repeatedly in his letters. Galatians is essentially one long argument against requiring Torah observance for Gentiles. He called it “a different gospel” (Galatians 1:6-9) and warned that those trying to be justified by law “have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4).

But not everyone accepted the apostolic decision.

Enter the Ebionites, a Jewish-Christian sect that insisted on Torah observance for all believers. They required circumcision. They kept Sabbath and dietary laws. They were deeply suspicious of Paul, with some rejecting him entirely as a false apostle. The more extreme Ebionites denied Jesus’ divinity and the virgin birth, but the core issue wasn’t Christology. it was Torah.

The early church labeled them heretics. Church fathers like Irenaeus, Origen, and Eusebius condemned them. Not primarily for denying Jesus’ deity (though some did), but for requiring what the apostles had explicitly decided was unnecessary: Torah observance for Gentiles.

After the temple’s destruction in 70 AD, Jewish Christianity began to fade. By the 4th century, it was nearly extinct. Gentile Christianity became the dominant expression. The Ebionites disappeared into history.

Until now.

Modern Messianic Movement (1960s-Present)

Fast forward to the 1960s.

The Jesus Movement was sweeping through America. At the same time, ethnic pride movements were rising, Black Power, Chicano activism, and yes, Jewish cultural assertion. Jewish believers in Jesus found themselves caught between two identities. The church told them to assimilate, to stop being “so Jewish.” But they didn’t want to abandon their heritage.

The solution: Messianic synagogues. Jews for Jesus. Chosen People Ministries. Organizations that said, “You can be Jewish and believe in Jesus.”

By the 1980s and 90s, the movement had structure, congregations, conferences, theological frameworks. And then something shifted.

Gentiles started joining. Not just attending Messianic synagogues, but adopting Jewish practices themselves. Hebrew Roots was born.

Today, the movement spans a spectrum:

  • Mild: Appreciating Jewish context, maybe celebrating some festivals
  • Moderate: Keeping Sabbath, dietary laws, and festivals as obedience to God
  • Extreme: Requiring Torah for salvation, questioning Paul’s apostleship, rejecting the Trinity

But across the spectrum, certain claims remain consistent.

Core Claims of the Movement

Let me present these as neutrally as possible, because I want you to hear what they say before I examine it.

Claim 1: Torah Is Still Binding for Believers

“The law hasn’t been abolished, Jesus said so in Matthew 5:17. Believers should keep Sabbath (Saturday, not Sunday), follow biblical dietary laws (kosher), and observe the biblical festivals (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles). Not for salvation, but for sanctification and obedience.”

Claim 2: Gentile Christianity Lost Its Jewish Roots

“Constantine, the Council of Nicaea, and Roman influence corrupted the faith. Sunday worship replaced Sabbath. Christmas and Easter replaced biblical festivals. Greek philosophy (the Trinity, for some) distorted simple Hebrew truth. We’re recovering what was lost.”

Claim 3: We’re Restoring What the Early Church Practiced

“The first believers were Torah-observant Jews. Acts 15 didn’t abolish Torah, it just said Gentiles don’t need it for salvation. Paul himself kept Torah his whole life. We’re just doing what they did.”

Claim 4: Hebrew Names and Language Matter

“’Jesus’ is a corruption, possibly pagan. The real name is Yeshua. ‘God’ is generic, use Yahweh or YHWH. Hebrew is the holy language, the language of Scripture. Using it brings you closer to the original revelation.”

Claim 5: Modern Israel Is Prophetically Significant

“Israel’s rebirth in 1948 is the fulfillment of prophecy. Supporting Israel politically and spiritually is a biblical mandate. The church replaced Israel at its own peril, we’re correcting that error.”

These aren’t strawmen. These are the actual claims you’ll hear from Messianic Judaism and Hebrew Roots teachers across platforms.

Now here’s what I’ve been finding as I dig deeper.

Questions That Won’t Go Away

I didn’t go into this research looking for problems. I went in genuinely curious. But the more I studied, reading their materials, comparing them to Scripture, tracing the history, the same questions kept surfacing. Questions I haven’t seen answered satisfactorily.

Question 1: The Ebionite Problem

The early church encountered a version of this theology. They were called Ebionites. They required Torah observance for Gentiles. They were suspicious of Paul. They claimed to represent authentic Jewish Christianity.

The church labeled them heretics.

The apostles at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) explicitly decided not to require Torah for Gentiles. Paul wrote Galatians specifically to combat people teaching what Messianic Judaism teaches today. The church fathers condemned the Ebionite framework, not just their Christology, but their Torah-centrality.

If the apostles and the early church rejected this theology, what authority does the modern movement have to revive it?

Question 2: The Paul Problem

Messianic Judaism claims to follow all of Scripture, including Paul’s letters. But Paul explicitly wrote:

  • “You are not under the law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14)
  • “Let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a religious festival, a New Moon celebration or a Sabbath day. These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ” (Colossians 2:16-17)
  • “By calling this covenant ‘new,’ he has made the first one obsolete” (Hebrews 8:13)

The movement constantly reinterprets Paul. “Not under law” becomes “not under condemnation.” “Shadow” becomes “don’t let Judaizers judge you for keeping Sabbath.” “Obsolete” becomes “only the sacrificial system, not Torah itself.”

At what point does constant reinterpretation to fit a predetermined conclusion become eisegesis? And if Paul meant what it sounds like he meant, doesn’t that dismantle the entire framework?

Question 3: Acts 15 and the Torah Question

The Jerusalem Council made a decision. After debate, James declared:

“It is my judgment, therefore, that we should not make it difficult for the Gentiles who are turning to God. Instead we should write to them, telling them to abstain from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals and from blood” (Acts 15:19-20).

Four requirements. That’s it.

No dietary laws beyond blood and strangled animals. No festivals. No circumcision.

If Torah observance was necessary for holy living, why didn’t the apostles include it? Why did they explicitly say “we should not make it difficult” by adding more requirements?

The movement says Acts 15 was about salvation, not sanctification. But the text doesn’t make that distinction. It says don’t burden Gentiles. Period.

Why does the movement overturn what the apostles decided?

Question 4: The Galatians 2:21 Problem

Paul wrote:

“I do not set aside the grace of God, for if righteousness could be gained through the law, Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21).

Let that sit for a moment.

If righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing.

The movement teaches Torah-keeping for sanctification, for righteousness, for holy living. But Paul’s logic is absolute: if righteousness comes through law at all, whether for justification or sanctification, then grace is nullified and Christ’s death was pointless.

How does the movement escape that condemnation?

Question 5: The Source Problem

I keep noticing something. Messianic Judaism and Hebrew Roots advocates frequently cite the Talmud, Midrash, and rabbinic sources. They learn from teachers who rejected Jesus as Messiah.

Rabbi Akiva, for example, a major figure in rabbinic Judaism who explicitly rejected Jesus and declared Bar Kokhba (a failed military leader) as Messiah. His teachings and the Midrash he influenced are cited as authoritative for understanding Scripture.

But these are post-Christian sources. Rabbinic Judaism developed after rejecting Jesus, in opposition to Christianity. The Talmud was compiled by people who denied the New Covenant.

Why would you learn covenant theology from people who rejected the covenant you claim to follow?

Why This Matters

I’m not writing this to attack anyone’s sincerity. I’ve met many people in Messianic Judaism and Hebrew Roots who are earnest, faithful believers trying to follow Scripture as best they understand it.

But frameworks matter. Theology has consequences.

If this movement is reviving a theology the early church explicitly rejected, that’s not a minor historical footnote. If it’s requiring practices the apostles said were unnecessary, that’s not “honoring Jewish roots,” that’s adding to the gospel.

And if Galatians 2:21 is right, that making righteousness dependent on law nullifies grace and makes Christ’s death pointless, then this isn’t just an alternative expression of Christian faith.

It’s a different gospel.

Over the next few months, I’ll be examining these questions in depth. Not to win arguments, but to test frameworks against Scripture. To trace systems back to their source and ask whether the foundation is sound.

A Word to Readers

If you’re in Messianic Judaism or Hebrew Roots, I’d love to hear how you reconcile these tensions.

If you’ve left the movement, I want to know what made you reconsider. What broke through? What questions couldn’t be answered?

And if you’re just learning about this for the first time, buckle up. This is going to be a thorough investigation.

Because Kingdom Code doesn’t do surface-level takes. We dig until we hit bedrock. We trace patterns to their source. We ask whether the foundation is Covenant or Babylon.

Messianic Judaism claims to be Covenant restoration.

Let’s find out if that’s true.

If you found this helpful, share it. If you have questions, ask them. And if you’re in the movement and think I’ve misrepresented something, tell me. I want to get this right.
